longQuestions: (a) A continuous random variable X has a uniform (rectangular) distribution on (a, b) if f(x) = 1/(b − a) for a < x < b and 0 otherwise.
(b) Mean = ∫ₐᵇ x/(b−a) dx = (a + b)/2; E(X²) = (a² + ab + b²)/3, so variance = (b − a)²/12.
The normal distribution is a continuous, bell-shaped, symmetric distribution with p.d.f. f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))] e^{−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)}, −∞ < x < ∞, with parameters μ (mean) and σ (S.D).

Importance: many natural and social measurements (heights, weights, errors, marks) are approximately normal; it is the basis of the central limit theorem — sampling distributions of means are approximately normal; binomial and Poisson distributions approach it; and most tests of significance and confidence intervals are based on it.
Definition: X is normally distributed with mean μ and variance σ² if f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))] e^{−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)}, −∞ < x < ∞.

Properties: bell-shaped and symmetric about μ; mean = median = mode; the tails never touch the x-axis; total area = 1; skewness = 0 and kurtosis (β₂) = 3; Q₁ and Q₃ are equidistant from the mean; M.D ≈ (4/5)σ and Q.D ≈ (2/3)σ; about 68.3%, 95.4% and 99.7% of the area lie within μ ± σ, μ ± 2σ and μ ± 3σ.
Standard normal variable: Z = (X − μ)/σ, which has mean 0 and S.D 1.
Standard normal distribution: the normal distribution of Z, φ(z) = (1/√(2π)) e^{−z²/2}.

Role: any normal variable can be changed to Z, so one table of areas (Z-table) gives probabilities for all normal distributions; it is also used to compare scores from different distributions and in tests of significance.

Ordinate method of fitting: (1) find the mean x̄ and S.D σ of the given data (N = 1000); (2) for each class mid-point x compute z = (x − x̄)/σ; (3) find the ordinate φ(z) from the table of normal ordinates; (4) expected frequency = (N·h/σ)·φ(z), where h is the class width; (5) round off and compare with observed frequencies.

Fit by the same method: compute x̄ and σ of the data, then for each mid-point x find z = (x − x̄)/σ, the ordinate φ(z), and expected frequency = (N·h/σ)·φ(z) (or, by the area method, N × area of each class under the normal curve).
